extracted.intended_audience: readers of Montaigne; educated readers interested in moral philosophy and ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the evaluative principles Montaigne uses in this essay (on virtue, cruelty, animals, and learning). Focus is on how actions, character, and institutions are judged in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue strengthened by trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is much strengthened by being attacked or tested; one should seek occasions (pain, necessity, contempt) to put resolutions and reason to the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites the maxim “Multum sibi adjicit virtus lacessita” (Virtue is much strengthened by combats) and examples such as Epaminondas refusing riches to contend with poverty, Socrates enduring a scolding wife, and Metellus facing Saturninus. Use historical exemplars to judge whether virtue is merely passive or robustly exercised; consider whether an agent sought or endured hardship to form or prove virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: True virtue refuses facility
rubrics_metrics.description: True virtue does not take the easy, smooth, descending way; it requires a rough and stormy passage and either external or internal difficulties to be tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that virtue 'refuses facility for a companion' and that easy, untroubled dispositions that simply do no wrong may be innocent but not truly virtuous. When evaluating character, distinguish effortless goodness from the active, tested excellence expected of a 'true' virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish habit-formed virtue from mere innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: A condition that makes a man innocent (free from doing ill) is not the same as being virtuous (apt to do well); absence of vice isn't necessarily active goodness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns that some virtues (chastity, sobriety, temperance) may arise from personal defects or temperament rather than deliberative moral strength. Labeling: 'innocent but not virtuous.' Evaluate whether moral behavior stems from cultivated habit and reasoned discipline or merely from natural disposition/fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge death by the life that precedes it
rubrics_metrics.description: Every death ought to hold proportion with the life before it; a strong death attached to a feeble life likely arises from a feeble cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle 'I always interpret the death by the life preceding' to assess the moral significance of someone's death (e.g., Cato, Socrates). Do not overvalue an isolated show of firmness in death if the preceding life lacked substantive virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of actions and attribution of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging a particular action, consider the circumstances and the whole person performing it before giving it a name; fortune, ignorance, or misperception may be mistaken for prudence or courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points out that friends often call his prudence 'fortune' and his courage 'judgment.' He also notes that 'constancy in danger' may sometimes arise from not apprehending peril. Always assess background, temperament, and situation to avoid misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that apparent virtue may be ignorance or defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent virtuous effects (e.g., contempt of death, patience) may sometimes be produced by lack of apprehension, stupidity, or other defects rather than genuine moral excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives the example of raw soldiers rushing into danger and says that want of apprehension sometimes counterfeits virtuous effects. Scrutinize the causal explanation for conduct before praising it as virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the origin of good: nature, upbringing, or discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a person's good qualities come from chance of birth, domestic example, education, natural temperament, or conscious discipline and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne candidly attributes his own 'good' in part to fortunate birth and upbringing rather than to reason or law. Use biographical and developmental evidence (family, education, innate temperament) to evaluate the source and stability of virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vices are not necessarily inseparable; evaluate them singly
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the idea that when the wicked man does wickedly he does so by all the vices together; one may follow some vices and shun others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne disputes the Stoic/Peripatetic over-generalization and uses Aristotle/Socrates/Stilpo examples where individuals correct certain inclinations by discipline. Evaluate each vice separately and avoid assuming a universal bundle of moral failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning is valuable but not the sovereign good
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is a great accomplishment and should be respected, but it should not be adored as the supreme good or considered the mother of all virtue; ignorance does not automatically entail vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne says he 'loves them well, but I do not adore them' and rejects claims that all vice proceeds from ignorance. When judging conduct or policy, weigh learning alongside other virtues and factors rather than elevating erudition above moral character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty is the extreme of vice; punishments should avoid excessive torment
rubrics_metrics.description: All that exceeds a simple death appears pure cruelty; inflicting insufferable torments on the living is inhumane, and exemplary severity could be exercised on the dead rather than the living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne condemns spectacle-driven cruelty (cutting in quarters, boiling) and suggests less horrific deterrents (e.g., exposing bodies rather than torturing). Use humane principles in justice: avoid inflicting agonizing tortures and consider the psychological and moral harms of public spectacles of pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity and benignity toward animals and plants
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a general duty of humanity not only to creatures with sense but even to trees and plants; kindness and regard toward animals and the natural world are owed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites customs (Turkish alms for beasts, Roman care for geese, Athenians freeing work animals, Pythagorean buying of animals) and laments bloodthirstiness in hunting and spectacles. When evaluating moral conduct, include treatment of animals as a measure of compassion; avoid taking pleasure in the slaughter or torment of defenseless creatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about deriving moral credit from spectacles or public reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public spectators' reactions (doleful cry at quartering, delight at gladiatorial shows) are unreliable moral signals; public appetite for spectacles can normalize cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne describes how crowds react and how spectacle breeds further cruelty. Be skeptical of popular approval as evidence of moral rightness; consider how collective entertainment may distort moral judgment.
